must_remember: When a ray of light is incident on an anisotropic crystal like calcite ($	ext{CaCO}_3$), it splits into an Ordinary (O) ray and an Extraordinary (E) ray.
The O-ray obeys ordinary laws of refraction, has a spherical wavefront, and constant refractive index $mu_o$.
The E-ray does not obey Snell's law in general, has an ellipsoidal wavefront, and its refractive index $mu_e$ varies with direction.
In negative uniaxial crystals (e.g., calcite), $v_e > v_o$ and $mu_e < mu_o$.
In positive uniaxial crystals (e.g., quartz), $v_e < v_o$ and $mu_e > mu_o$.
Along the optic axis, the velocities of both O-ray and E-ray are identical ($v_o = v_e$), resulting in no double refraction.
A Quarter-Wave Plate produces a phase shift of $pi/2$ and has a thickness $d_{QWP} =  rac{lambda_0}{4 |mu_o - mu_e|}$.
A Half-Wave Plate produces a phase shift of $pi$ and has a thickness $d_{HWP} =  rac{lambda_0}{2 |mu_o - mu_e|}$.

glossary.meaning: A refracted ray in a birefringent crystal that obeys ordinary laws of refraction and travels with a constant speed in all directions.
A refracted ray in a birefringent crystal that does not obey Snell's law and travels with a velocity dependent on the direction relative to the optic axis.
A specific direction inside an anisotropic crystal along which the velocities of the O-ray and E-ray are identical, causing no double refraction.
A birefringent crystal in which the velocity of the E-ray is greater than that of the O-ray ($mu_e < mu_o$), such as calcite.
A birefringent crystal in which the velocity of the E-ray is less than that of the O-ray ($mu_e > mu_o$), such as quartz.
The phase difference $Delta phi$ introduced between the O-ray and E-ray upon traversing a thickness $d$ of a birefringent crystal plate.
